Servlet Fundamentals

This content was generated with the assistance of AI and should be verified against the official documentation before being relied on in production.

The reference material consulted while preparing these pages is listed in the section bibliography.

This page is written against Jakarta Servlet 6.1 (Jakarta EE 11), the specification that Apache Tomcat 11.0.26 implements together with Jakarta Pages 4.0, Jakarta Expression Language 6.0 and Jakarta Standard Tag Library 3.0, on Java 21 (the specifications need Java 17 or later). Everything was verified on 2026-10-08: the facts against the Servlet 6.1 specification, its Javadoc and the Tomcat 11.0 documentation, and every example by building it into a Maven WAR and running it on Tomcat 11.0.26 with curl; the outputs shown are the outputs that run produced. Servlets are the layer underneath both halves of this section. A JSP is translated into a servlet (JSP Lifecycle and Translation), and Struts 7 is a filter plus a set of servlet-API calls, so the vocabulary on this page (request, response, scope, filter, dispatcher, mapping, error page) is the vocabulary the rest of the section uses. The running scenario is the Bookshelf, a small catalogue of books that grows from a servlet that lists three titles into an application with sessions, cookies, filters, listeners, error pages and a cover-image upload.

What a Servlet Is and Where It Runs

A servlet is a Java class that a servlet container (Tomcat, Jetty, GlassFish, WildFly and others) instantiates, calls and destroys, in order to turn a request into a response. The specification defines the contract between container and application: the Servlet interface, the request and response objects, the application-wide ServletContext, the packaging of a web application as a WAR, and the deployment descriptor web.xml. Almost every Java web technology sits on top of that contract. A JSP page is compiled into an HttpJspPage servlet, Struts 2 installs a servlet filter, Spring MVC is a single DispatcherServlet, and the Jakarta Faces runtime is the FacesServlet.

The container does the work that is the same for every application: it listens on a socket, parses HTTP, selects the web application and the servlet from the URL, manages threads, tracks sessions, applies filters, handles errors and cleans up. The application supplies only the code that is different.

Table 1. Servlet versions, Jakarta EE releases and the Tomcat lines that implement them (Tomcat "Which Version" page, 2026-10-08)
Servlet Jakarta EE Tomcat line Notes

6.1

EE 11

11.0.x (Java 17 or later)

Current. Pages 4.0, EL 6.0. Redirect control, HttpSession.Accessor, HTTP/2 server push deprecated, jakarta.servlet.error.method, Charset overloads of setCharacterEncoding

6.0

EE 10

10.1.x (Java 11 or later)

Removed the long-deprecated API (SingleThreadModel, HttpSessionContext, HttpUtils), generic cookie attributes (SameSite), RFC 6265, HttpServletRequest.getRequestId

5.0

EE 9

10.0.x (end of life 2022-10-31)

Only the namespace change javax.servlet to jakarta.servlet

4.0

EE 8

9.0.x (Java 8 or later; end of support not before 2027-03-31)

Last javax.servlet line; HTTP/2 push, HttpServletMapping

3.1

Java EE 7

8.5.x (end of life 2024-03-31)

Non-blocking I/O, protocol upgrade; this is what many 2015-era tutorials target

Source: Apache Tomcat — Which Version Do I Want?

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — Appendix A, Changes Since 6.0

A web application written for the servlet API needs only two Maven dependencies at compile time, both with scope provided because the container supplies them. The Bookshelf of this page uses the same pom.xml shape as the Getting Started page of this section.

The compile-time dependency of every example on this page
<dependency>
    <groupId>jakarta.servlet</groupId>
    <artifactId>jakarta.servlet-api</artifactId>
    <version>6.1.0</version>
    <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — specification page

The Bookshelf Used on This Page

All the examples below are classes of one WAR, deployed under the context path /g2-servlet on Tomcat 11.0.26 with the WAR file named g2-servlet.war. The classes live in the package org.example.bookshelf; imports and the package line are left out of the listings. The table lists what each class demonstrates and where the page explains it.

Table 2. The classes of the example WAR
Class Mapping Concept

LifecycleServlet

/lifecycle

/redirects, /books/*

ScopesServlet, CartServlet, PrefsServlet

/scopes, /cart, /prefs

scopes, ServletContext, sessions, cookies

TimingFilter, TrimFilter, FooterFilter, DispatchTraceFilter, AdminFilter

(none)

UploadServlet, AsyncServlet, LogServlet, HomeServlet

The HTTP Contract Behind a Servlet

Servlets implement a thin layer over HTTP, so a few protocol facts decide how every servlet is written. HTTP is a request/response protocol: the client sends a request line, headers and optionally a body, and the server answers with a status line, headers and a body. It is stateless: nothing in the protocol links two requests, which is why the servlet API adds sessions on top. The raw exchange for a form POST to the example’s /search servlet is:

curl -sv -d 'title=Dune&tag=sf' http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/search -o /dev/null
> POST /g2-servlet/search HTTP/1.1
> Host: localhost:18080
> Accept: */*
> Content-Length: 17
> Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
>
< HTTP/1.1 200
< Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8
< Content-Length: 302

Every line maps to an accessor of HttpServletRequest or a setter of HttpServletResponse: the method and path are getMethod() and getRequestURI(), Host is getServerName(), Content-Type is getContentType(), and the body is the source of getParameter. The same facts, in table form:

Table 3. GET versus POST as a servlet author sees them
GET POST

Meaning

Retrieve a representation; safe and idempotent

Submit data for processing; changes state

Data

In the query string, visible in logs, history and Referer

In the body, application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data

Servlet method

doGet

doPost

Caching and bookmarks

Cacheable, bookmarkable, repeatable by crawlers and prefetchers

Not cached; a browser asks before re-sending

Never use it for

Anything with a side effect, or secrets in the URL

Idempotent lookups that people want to bookmark

Answer after success

200 with the representation

303 redirect to a GET (Post/Redirect/Get)

Servlets are hosted by a servlet container: a server such as Tomcat that implements the Servlet contract and adds HTTP connectors, class loading, session management and deployment. Applets, which ran in the browser, played the other role in 1990s pages; servlets run only on the server and send the browser plain HTML or data.

Source: RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 1.2 What is a Servlet Container

The Servlet Lifecycle and the Threading Model

The container manages every servlet through a fixed lifecycle expressed by three methods of the Servlet interface. HttpServlet and GenericServlet implement it, so an application normally overrides init() (the no-argument convenience), a doXxx method and destroy().

Table 4. The servlet lifecycle (specification chapter 2)
Phase Container call What the application should know

Load and instantiate

the class is loaded and a public no-argument constructor runs

At startup or lazily on the first request. loadOnStartup (or <load-on-startup>) asks for startup; a non-negative value means "at deployment, lowest numbers first"

Initialize

init(ServletConfig) exactly once

Read init parameters, open expensive resources. If it throws ServletException or UnavailableException, the servlet is not put in service, destroy() is not called, and the container may try a fresh instance later

Serve

service(request, response) for every request, possibly on many threads at once

HttpServlet.service dispatches to doGet, doPost, and the other doXxx methods; a servlet may legitimately handle no request at all

Destroy

destroy() once, after all requests have left service

Release resources. It runs at undeploy or shutdown, or when an UnavailableException marks the servlet permanently unavailable

The rule that shapes every design is in section 2.2 of the specification: unless the application is marked distributable, the container uses one instance per servlet declaration. Every request that reaches that declaration runs on a different thread but calls the same object. Fields of a servlet are therefore shared mutable state, exactly as if they were static.

A servlet with one shared counter, read-only configuration and a destroy hook
@WebServlet(urlPatterns = "/lifecycle", loadOnStartup = 1,
        initParams = @WebInitParam(name = "greeting", value = "Hello from init"))
public class LifecycleServlet extends HttpServlet {

    private final AtomicInteger hits = new AtomicInteger(); // shared by every request thread
    private String greeting;                                 // written once in init, read-only afterwards

    @Override
    public void init() throws ServletException {
        greeting = getInitParameter("greeting");
        EventLog.of(getServletContext()).add("LifecycleServlet.init, instance " + System.identityHashCode(this));
    }

    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        resp.getWriter().printf("%s%ninstance=%d hits=%d thread=%s%n", greeting,
                System.identityHashCode(this), hits.incrementAndGet(), Thread.currentThread().getName());
    }

    @Override
    public void destroy() {
        getServletContext().log("LifecycleServlet.destroy after " + hits.get() + " hits");
    }
}

The shared counter is an AtomicInteger, and greeting is written once in init before any request thread can see the servlet, so both are safe. Requesting the servlet three times, and then sixty more requests that the container served on twenty parallel client connections, shows one instance and a count that never loses an update:

curl -s http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/lifecycle
seq 1 60 | xargs -P 20 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/lifecycle
curl -s http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/lifecycle | tail -1
Hello from init
instance=1266317426 hits=2 thread=http-nio-18080-exec-18
instance=1266317426 hits=64 thread=http-nio-18080-exec-17

The instance number is identical in every response, while the thread names (http-nio-18080-exec-N) are different threads of Tomcat’s pool. The servlet was marked loadOnStartup = 1, so init ran at deployment, before the first request: the trace servlet of the example (/log) shows it, and redeploying the WAR makes Tomcat call destroy, which the example writes to Tomcat’s application log with ServletContext.log:

contextInitialized: 3 books, title=Bookshelf
LifecycleServlet.init, instance 1266317426
...
INFO [Catalina-utility-2] org.apache.catalina.core.ApplicationContext.log LifecycleServlet.destroy after 64 hits

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 2.3 Servlet Life Cycle

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 2.2 Number of Instances

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 2.3.3.1 Multithreading Issues

The specification states the thread-safety rules in several places. They are collected here because they are the source of most production bugs.

Table 5. What is shared between threads, and what is not
Object Thread-safe? Rule

Servlet and filter instances

shared by all requests

Keep fields immutable or thread-safe; never store per-request data in fields. The specification advises against synchronizing service because of the performance cost

HttpServletRequest, HttpServletResponse, PrintWriter, ServletOutputStream

no

Objects vended from the request or response must be assumed non-thread-safe (section 7.7.1); hand them to another thread only through startAsync

HttpSession attribute collection

the container protects its own structure

The objects you store are your responsibility: two requests of one user can run at once (two browser tabs, an AJAX call)

ServletContext attributes

the container protects the map

Stored objects must be thread-safe, as in the example AtomicInteger, CopyOnWriteArrayList and synchronized EventLog

Listener instances

one instance per declaration

Application-scoped listeners need the same care as servlets

SingleThreadModel, the old escape hatch that made a container serialize calls to a servlet, was deprecated for years and removed in Servlet 6.0. A legacy servlet that implements it no longer compiles against the 6.x API; the fix is to remove the instance state, not to add synchronized to every method.

An UnavailableException thrown from service tells the container that the servlet cannot serve, permanently or for a number of seconds. The container then answers 404 (permanent) or 503 with a Retry-After header (temporary) without calling the servlet, and it is allowed to treat both kinds as permanent.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 2.3.3.2 Exceptions During Request Handling

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 7.7.1 Threading Issues

HttpServlet, HTTP Methods and Method Handling

HttpServlet.service reads the HTTP method and calls the matching method. A servlet overrides only the methods it supports, and the base class answers the rest.

Table 6. The doXxx methods of HttpServlet
Method Behaviour

doGet

Safe, idempotent retrieval. Override getLastModified to enable conditional GET (If-Modified-Since) handling

doPost

Form submissions and state changes; the usual target of a Post/Redirect/Get flow

doPut, doDelete, doPatch

Servlet 6.0 added PATCH support to the specification; the container routes them to the corresponding method if you override it

doHead

By default calls doGet and lets the container drop the body, so the headers always match. The legacy behaviour that wrapped the response is deprecated and only enabled by the jakarta.servlet.http.legacyDoHead init parameter

doOptions

Answers with an Allow header built from the methods you overrode

doTrace

Echoes the request, excluding the headers isSensitiveHeader lists (Authorization, Cookie, X-Forwarded, Forwarded, Proxy-Authorization)

CONNECT

A proxy method. By default the container rejects it with 501 and never passes it to a filter or servlet

A method the servlet does not override is answered by the base class, as the example shows with LifecycleServlet, which has only doGet:

curl -sI  http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/lifecycle | head -2
curl -si -X POST    http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/lifecycle | head -1
curl -si -X OPTIONS http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/lifecycle | grep -i '^allow'
curl -si -X TRACE   http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/lifecycle | head -1
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8
HTTP/1.1 405
Allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
HTTP/1.1 405

HEAD works without any code, POST gets 405, and OPTIONS reports exactly the methods the class implements. TRACE never reaches doTrace, because Tomcat’s HTTP connector rejects it with 405 unless the connector attribute allowTrace is set.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 2.1.1 HTTP Specific Request Handling Methods

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 2.1.2 HEAD Method

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — HttpServlet

Source: Apache Tomcat 11 — HTTP connector, allowTrace

Requests: Parameters, Headers, Paths and Attributes

An HttpServletRequest gives the servlet read access to everything the client sent and a small writable map of attributes. The accessors fall into five groups.

Table 7. The main request accessors
Group Methods and rules

Request line

getMethod(), getRequestURI() (the raw path, still percent-encoded, without the query), getRequestURL() (scheme, host, port and path), getQueryString(), getProtocol(), getScheme(), isSecure()

Path elements

getContextPath(), getServletPath(), getPathInfo(). The request URI is always context path plus servlet path plus path info (plus path parameters such as ;jsessionid), see the mapping section

Parameters

getParameter(name), getParameterValues(name), getParameterMap(), getParameterNames(). They merge the query string and, for a form POST with application/x-www-form-urlencoded, the body. Multipart text fields are also parameters when the servlet has @MultipartConfig

Headers

getHeader(name) (first value, name is case-insensitive), getHeaders(name) (all values), getHeaderNames(), getIntHeader, getDateHeader; getLocale() and getLocales() parse Accept-Language; getContentType(), getContentLength(), getCharacterEncoding()

Body and connection

getReader() or getInputStream() (one of them, never both), getRemoteAddr(), getServerName(), getServerPort(), and the 6.0 identifiers getRequestId(), getProtocolRequestId() and getServletConnection()

Attributes

setAttribute, getAttribute, removeAttribute: per-request storage used to pass the model from a controller servlet to a view

The one rule about parameters that surprises people is ordering. Parameters are parsed on the first call to any parameter method, and a form body can be consumed only once. If a servlet or filter reads the body with getReader() or getInputStream() first, the container has nothing left to parse and getParameter returns null for form fields. In Servlet 6.1 a failure during parsing (a malformed body, an exceeded limit) makes the parameter methods throw a runtime exception, so a filter that touches parameters must be prepared to catch it (specification change log, issue 431).

The next servlet prints what the container exposes for a request. It is mapped to /search and, as the filter section will show, runs behind a request wrapper that trims whitespace around every parameter value.

Reading parameters, headers and locale
@WebServlet("/search")
public class SearchServlet extends HttpServlet {

    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        handle(req, resp);
    }

    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        handle(req, resp);
    }

    private void handle(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain");           // the charset comes from web.xml (UTF-8)
        PrintWriter out = resp.getWriter();
        out.println("method=" + req.getMethod() + " query=" + req.getQueryString());
        out.println("request encoding=" + req.getCharacterEncoding() + " type=" + req.getContentType());
        out.println("title=" + req.getParameter("title"));
        out.println("tag=" + Arrays.toString(req.getParameterValues("tag")));
        Map<String, String[]> sorted = new TreeMap<>(req.getParameterMap());
        sorted.forEach((k, v) -> out.println("  param " + k + " -> " + Arrays.toString(v)));
        out.println("Accept-Language=" + req.getHeader("Accept-Language"));
        out.println("locale=" + req.getLocale() + " locales=" + Collections.list(req.getLocales()));
        out.println("Accept (all values)=" + Collections.list(req.getHeaders("Accept")));
        out.println("User-Agent present=" + (req.getHeader("User-Agent") != null));
        out.println("response encoding=" + resp.getCharacterEncoding() + " locale=" + resp.getLocale()
                + " (" + Locale.getDefault() + " default)");
    }
}
curl -s -H 'Accept-Language: es-ES,es;q=0.9,en;q=0.5' \
  'http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/search?title=%20Dune%20&tag=sf&tag=classic'
method=GET query=title=%20Dune%20&tag=sf&tag=classic
request encoding=UTF-8 type=null
title=Dune
tag=[sf, classic]
  param tag -> [sf, classic]
  param title -> [Dune]
Accept-Language=es-ES,es;q=0.9,en;q=0.5
locale=es_ES locales=[es_ES, es, en]
Accept (all values)=[*/*]
User-Agent present=true
response encoding=UTF-8 locale=en_US (en_US default)

getQueryString() returns the raw text, getParameter("title") returns the decoded and trimmed value Dune, getParameterValues("tag") keeps both values in order, and getLocales() returns the client’s languages in preference order. The request encoding line is UTF-8 and the type is null because the deployment descriptor of the example sets <request-character-encoding>, as the next section explains.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 3.1 HTTP Protocol Parameters

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 3.4 Headers

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 3.3 Attributes

Reading Headers: Content Negotiation in a Controller

Headers drive content negotiation. The BookServlet of the example serves the same catalogue as HTML or JSON depending on the Accept header, and sets Vary: Accept so that a shared cache keeps the two representations apart.

BookServlet.doGet: one URL, two representations, path info for the id
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws ServletException, IOException {
        Catalogue catalogue = Catalogue.of(getServletContext());
        String info = req.getPathInfo();                      // null for /books, "/2" for /books/2

        if (info == null || info.equals("/")) {
            req.setAttribute("books", catalogue.all());
            req.setAttribute("csrf", csrfToken(req.getSession()));
            if (wantsJson(req)) {
                resp.setContentType("application/json");
                resp.setHeader("Vary", "Accept");
                resp.getWriter().write(toJson(catalogue));
                return;
            }
            resp.setHeader("Vary", "Accept");
            req.getRequestDispatcher("/WEB-INF/views/books.jsp").forward(req, resp);
            return;
        }

        long id;
        try {
            id = Long.parseLong(info.substring(1));
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST, "Book ids are numbers");
            return;
        }
        Optional<Book> book = catalogue.find(id);
        if (book.isEmpty()) {
            resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_NOT_FOUND);
            return;
        }
        req.setAttribute("book", book.get());
        req.getRequestDispatcher("/WEB-INF/views/book.jsp").forward(req, resp);
    }
curl -si -H 'Accept: application/json' http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/books | sed -n 1,5p
curl -si http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/books/99 | sed -n 1,2p
curl -si http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/books/abc | sed -n 1,2p
HTTP/1.1 200
Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=B190D8D3...; Path=/g2-servlet; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Vary: Accept
Content-Type: application/json;charset=UTF-8
[{"id":1,"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert","year":1965},...]
HTTP/1.1 404
HTTP/1.1 400

The Set-Cookie line appears because the servlet calls req.getSession() to create the CSRF token; the next sections explain that header. /books/99 is answered by sendError(404) and /books/abc by sendError(400, ...), and the error page mechanism described later renders both.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 3.6 Request Path Elements

Character Encoding

Encoding is the most common reason for garbled accented characters in a servlet application, and the specification’s defaults are older than the web.

Table 8. The encoding rules of Servlet 6.1 (sections 3.13 and 5.6)
Situation Rule

Request body, application/x-www-form-urlencoded, no charset in Content-Type

The container must decode with US-ASCII and treat %nn values as ISO-8859-1; getCharacterEncoding() returns null to show the charset is unknown

Any other request body without charset

ISO-8859-1, unless the application or container configured something else

Configure the request encoding

<request-character-encoding> in web.xml, ServletContext.setRequestCharacterEncoding at startup, or request.setCharacterEncoding before any parameter is read or any input consumed; calling it afterwards has no effect

Response with no encoding set

ISO-8859-1 for the writer

Configure the response encoding

<response-character-encoding>, ServletContext.setResponseCharacterEncoding, response.setCharacterEncoding, a charset in setContentType, or setLocale with a locale-encoding mapping. Calls after getWriter() or after commit are ignored

URL path and query string

Decoded as UTF-8 per section 12.1; containers may offer a vendor option (Tomcat’s connector has URIEncoding)

Servlet 6.1 API

setCharacterEncoding(Charset) overloads on ServletRequest and ServletResponse (issue 415) next to the String forms

A request that did not declare a charset is the dangerous one, because curl, many mobile clients and hand-written fetch calls omit it. The example declares both encodings once for the whole application:

web.xml: one declaration, every servlet, filter and JSP
<request-character-encoding>UTF-8</request-character-encoding>
<response-character-encoding>UTF-8</response-character-encoding>

Posting Ñandú in UTF-8 to /search shows the effect, and /search-legacy, which forces the old default with the Servlet 6.1 Charset overload, shows the "before":

The "before": forcing ISO-8859-1 garbles UTF-8 input
@WebServlet("/search-legacy")
public class LegacyEncodingServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        req.setCharacterEncoding(StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1);   // Servlet 6.1 overload taking a Charset
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        resp.getWriter().println("title=" + req.getParameter("title"));
    }
}
curl -s -d 'title=Ñandú' http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/search | sed -n 3p
curl -s -d 'title=Ñandú' http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/search-legacy
curl -s --data-binary 'title=Ñandú' -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded; charset=ISO-8859-1' \
  http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/search | sed -n 3p
title=Ñandú
title=ÃandÃº
title=ÃandÃº

The second line is the classic mojibake: UTF-8 bytes decoded as ISO-8859-1. The third line shows that an explicit charset in the Content-Type header of the request wins over the default of web.xml, so a client that declares the wrong charset is believed. curl -d sends no charset at all; that is what browsers do for plain form posts, which is why the <request-character-encoding> default matters. JSP pages declare their own encodings (pageEncoding, contentType) and Character Encoding covers that side.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 3.13 Request Data Encoding

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 5.6 Internationalization

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — ServletRequest

Responses: Status, Headers, Body and Buffering

The response is the mirror image of the request. A servlet sets the status, adds headers, and writes the body to a PrintWriter (getWriter(), characters) or a ServletOutputStream (getOutputStream(), bytes). It may use one or the other for a response, never both, or the second call throws IllegalStateException.

Table 9. The main response methods
Group Methods and rules

Status

setStatus(int): a normal status, no error page. sendError(int) and sendError(int, String): an error status, clears the buffer, commits, and lets the error page mechanism take over. Servlet 6.1 adds constants for 308, 421, 422 and 426 (SC_PERMANENT_REDIRECT, SC_MISDIRECTED_REQUEST, SC_UNPROCESSABLE_CONTENT, SC_UPGRADE_REQUIRED)

Headers

setHeader, addHeader, setIntHeader, setDateHeader, containsHeader, getHeader. 6.1 clarifies what null and empty names or values do

Type and encoding

setContentType("text/html;charset=UTF-8"), setCharacterEncoding, setLocale, setContentLength, setContentLengthLong

Cookies and URLs

addCookie, encodeURL, encodeRedirectURL; the old encodeUrl and encodeRedirectUrl spellings were removed in 6.0

Buffer

setBufferSize, getBufferSize, isCommitted, flushBuffer, reset, resetBuffer

Redirect

sendRedirect(String) and the 6.1 overloads, next section

The container may buffer output. The status line and headers are written to the wire when the response is committed: the buffer fills, flushBuffer() is called, the content length is reached, or sendError or sendRedirect is called. Before the commit the servlet may change anything (reset() clears body, status and headers, resetBuffer() clears only the body); after it, the rules are unforgiving. The next servlet exercises each of them.

Committing a response, and what a late change does
@WebServlet("/buffer")
public class BufferServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        resp.setBufferSize(16 * 1024);                       // a hint: the container may give more, never less
        PrintWriter out = resp.getWriter();
        out.println("bufferSize>=16384: " + (resp.getBufferSize() >= 16 * 1024));
        switch (String.valueOf(req.getParameter("mode"))) {
            case "reset" -> {
                out.println("draft that will be discarded");
                resp.resetBuffer();                            // clears the body, keeps status and headers
                out.println("final body, committed=" + resp.isCommitted());
            }
            case "late-header" -> {
                out.println("first line");
                resp.flushBuffer();                            // commits: status line and headers are on the wire
                resp.setHeader("X-Too-Late", "1");             // silently ignored
                resp.setStatus(500);                           // silently ignored
                out.println("committed=" + resp.isCommitted());
            }
            case "late-error" -> {
                out.println("first line");
                resp.flushBuffer();
                try {
                    resp.sendError(500, "too late");
                } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
                    out.println("sendError after commit -> IllegalStateException");
                }
                try {
                    resp.resetBuffer();
                } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
                    out.println("resetBuffer after commit -> IllegalStateException");
                }
            }
            case "late-session" -> {
                out.println("first line");
                resp.flushBuffer();
                try {
                    req.getSession();                              // would need a Set-Cookie header
                    out.println("session created, id from cookie=" + req.isRequestedSessionIdFromCookie());
                } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
                    out.println("getSession after commit -> IllegalStateException");
                }
            }
            default -> out.println("modes: reset, late-header, late-error, late-session");
        }
    }
}
curl -si 'http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/buffer?mode=reset'
curl -si 'http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/buffer?mode=late-header'
curl -si 'http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/buffer?mode=late-error'
curl -si 'http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/buffer?mode=late-session'
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 28

final body, committed=false
HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

bufferSize>=16384: true
first line
committed=true
bufferSize>=16384: true
first line
sendError after commit -> IllegalStateException
resetBuffer after commit -> IllegalStateException
bufferSize>=16384: true
first line
getSession after commit -> IllegalStateException

The four outputs are the lesson of this section. With reset, the draft text and the earlier bufferSize line are gone and the response is a normal 200 with a Content-Length computed from what remained. With late-header, the setHeader("X-Too-Late", ...) and setStatus(500) calls after flushBuffer() were silently ignored: there is no X-Too-Late header, the status is still 200, and the body switched to chunked transfer because the length was unknown at commit time. With late-error and late-session, the calls that cannot be honoured throw IllegalStateException: sendError, sendRedirect, reset, resetBuffer and the creation of a session (which needs a Set-Cookie header). The specification calls this out for setBufferSize too, which must be called before any content is written.

The practical rules are: do all the work that can fail before writing, set headers and status first, create the session before writing, and call sendError or sendRedirect and then return. Frameworks such as Struts (Architecture & Request Lifecycle) and Spring MVC follow these rules by writing the view last.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 5.1 Buffering

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 5.5 Convenience Methods

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 5.7 Closure of the Response Object

Redirects, Including the Servlet 6.1 Controls

sendRedirect writes a Location header, sets a redirect status and commits the response. Before Servlet 6.1 the status was always 302 and the container always generated the body. Servlet 6.1 (issue 74) adds overloads that choose the status and control whether the buffer is cleared.

Table 10. The sendRedirect overloads
Signature Behaviour

sendRedirect(String location)

302, buffer cleared, short hypertext body generated by the container

sendRedirect(String location, boolean clearBuffer)

302, and false keeps the body that the servlet already wrote

sendRedirect(String location, int sc)

The status you choose, for example 303, 307 or 308

sendRedirect(String location, int sc, boolean clearBuffer)

Both

Relative locations are accepted. The specification (issue 275) lets a container send them as given, and Tomcat 11 does so by default unless the system property org.apache.catalina.STRICT_SERVLET_COMPLIANCE is true; it is controlled per context by useRelativeRedirects. A relative location without a leading slash is resolved against the current request URI, one with a leading slash against the container root, which is why the example builds the target from getContextPath().

Choosing the redirect status and keeping the body
@WebServlet("/redirects")
public class RedirectServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        String target = req.getContextPath() + "/books";
        switch (String.valueOf(req.getParameter("mode"))) {
            case "default" -> resp.sendRedirect(target);                                     // 302
            case "relative" -> resp.sendRedirect("books");                                   // relative to this request URI
            case "303" -> resp.sendRedirect(target, HttpServletResponse.SC_SEE_OTHER);       // 6.1: choose the status
            case "308" -> resp.sendRedirect(target, HttpServletResponse.SC_PERMANENT_REDIRECT); // 6.1 constant for 308
            case "keep-body" -> {
                resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
                resp.getWriter().print("my own redirect body");
                resp.sendRedirect(target, HttpServletResponse.SC_TEMPORARY_REDIRECT, false);  // 6.1: do not clear the buffer
            }
            case "bad" -> resp.sendRedirect("http://[bad host");                             // not a valid URL
            default -> resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST, "unknown mode");
        }
    }
}
for m in default relative 303 308 keep-body bad; do
  curl -si "http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/redirects?mode=$m" | sed -n '1,2p;/^Content-Length/p'
done
HTTP/1.1 302
Location: /g2-servlet/books
Content-Length: 0
HTTP/1.1 302
Location: books
Content-Length: 0
HTTP/1.1 303
Location: /g2-servlet/books
Content-Length: 0
HTTP/1.1 308
Location: /g2-servlet/books
Content-Length: 0
HTTP/1.1 307
Location: /g2-servlet/books
Content-Length: 20
HTTP/1.1 302
Location: http://[bad host
Content-Length: 0

The keep-body response (the last one) carries the 20 bytes my own redirect body that the servlet wrote, because the false argument stopped the container from clearing them. The Location values are relative, Tomcat’s default; the relative mode shows that the container passes the string through unchanged. The specification says a location that cannot be converted to a valid URL makes sendRedirect throw IllegalArgumentException; Tomcat 11.0.26, with relative redirects enabled, did not reject the malformed http://[bad host that the bad mode sends (the last response above).

The status code matters for forms. After a POST that changed state, answer with 303 See Other so the browser follows with a GET and a refresh cannot repeat the post (the Post/Redirect/Get pattern). 307 and 308 instruct the client to repeat the same method and body, which is right for moving an API endpoint but wrong for form submissions. BookServlet.doPost uses sendRedirect(..., SC_SEE_OTHER) and the walkthrough at the end of this page shows it.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — HttpServletResponse.sendRedirect(String, int, boolean)

Source: Apache Tomcat 11 — Context, useRelativeRedirects

Scopes and the ServletContext

Data in a servlet application lives in one of four scopes, each with its own lifetime and sharing. The scope names are the same ones JSP and EL use, so the model built by a servlet is what the view reads.

Table 11. The scopes of a web application
Scope Object Lifetime Visible to

Page

PageContext (JSP only)

one execution of one JSP page

that page and its tags (covered by Implicit Objects & Scopes)

Request

HttpServletRequest attributes

one request, including its forwards and includes

every servlet, filter and JSP that handles that request

Session

HttpSession attributes

until timeout, invalidate() or shutdown

every request of one client in this web application

Application

ServletContext attributes

until the web application stops

everything in the web application, all users

The ServletContext is the application’s window on the container. There is one per web application per JVM (section 4.2), reachable from a servlet with getServletContext(), from a filter or listener through its config or event, and from a JSP as the application object.

Table 12. What the ServletContext offers
Facility Methods and rules

Attributes

setAttribute, getAttribute, removeAttribute. Shared by all threads and all users. In a distributable application each JVM has its own copy, so context attributes are not a cluster-wide store

Initialization parameters

getInitParameter for <context-param> entries of web.xml: read-only configuration that is not tied to one servlet

Resources

getResource, getResourceAsStream, getResourcePaths read from the WAR (/WEB-INF/..., static files) with a path that starts with /; getRealPath may return null when the container does not unpack the WAR. The 6.1 Javadoc warns that these methods must treat the path as untrusted and canonicalize it

Information

getContextPath, getServerInfo, getMajorVersion/getMinorVersion (the API the container supports) and getEffectiveMajorVersion/getEffectiveMinorVersion (the version of the deployment descriptor)

MIME types

getMimeType(file) consults the <mime-mapping> entries and the container defaults

Dispatching

getRequestDispatcher(path), getNamedDispatcher(name)

Logging

log(String) and log(String, Throwable) write to the container’s application log

Session defaults

getSessionTimeout/setSessionTimeout (minutes), getSessionCookieConfig, setSessionTrackingModes

Encoding defaults

setRequestCharacterEncoding, setResponseCharacterEncoding (only during initialization)

Programmatic configuration

addServlet, addFilter, addListener and the Registration API, only while the context is being initialized

Temporary directory

the attribute jakarta.servlet.context.tempdir, a private writable directory per web application

The next servlet touches each of the four scopes and prints the facts the context knows:

Request, session and application scope, and a tour of ServletContext
@WebServlet("/scopes")
public class ScopesServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        ServletContext ctx = getServletContext();
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        PrintWriter out = resp.getWriter();

        req.setAttribute("who", "request");                          // gone when this request ends
        HttpSession session = req.getSession();                      // creates the session on first use
        AtomicInteger perSession = (AtomicInteger) session.getAttribute("count");
        if (perSession == null) {
            perSession = new AtomicInteger();
            session.setAttribute("count", perSession);               // survives across requests of one client
        }
        int total = ((AtomicInteger) ctx.getAttribute("visits")).incrementAndGet(); // shared by everyone

        out.println("request attribute who=" + req.getAttribute("who"));
        out.println("session count=" + perSession.incrementAndGet() + " (new=" + session.isNew() + ")");
        out.println("application visits=" + total);
        out.println("servlet API " + ctx.getMajorVersion() + "." + ctx.getMinorVersion()
                + ", effective " + ctx.getEffectiveMajorVersion() + "." + ctx.getEffectiveMinorVersion());
        out.println("context path=" + ctx.getContextPath() + " name=" + ctx.getServletContextName());
        out.println("context-param catalogue.title=" + ctx.getInitParameter("catalogue.title"));
        out.println("mime of cover.png=" + ctx.getMimeType("cover.png") + ", of feed.rss=" + ctx.getMimeType("feed.rss"));
        out.println("session timeout (minutes)=" + ctx.getSessionTimeout());
        out.println("request/response encoding=" + ctx.getRequestCharacterEncoding() + "/" + ctx.getResponseCharacterEncoding());
        out.println("resource /WEB-INF/web.xml exists=" + (ctx.getResource("/WEB-INF/web.xml") != null));
        out.println("resource /WEB-INF/../secret exists=" + (ctx.getResourceAsStream("/WEB-INF/../secret") != null));
    }
}
curl -s -c jar -b jar http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/scopes      # first request of this client
curl -s -c jar -b jar http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/scopes | sed -n 1,3p
curl -s http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/scopes | sed -n 1,3p       # another client, no cookie
request attribute who=request
session count=1 (new=true)
application visits=1
servlet API 6.1, effective 6.1
context path=/g2-servlet name=Bookshelf servlet fundamentals
context-param catalogue.title=Bookshelf
mime of cover.png=image/png, of feed.rss=application/rss+xml
session timeout (minutes)=30
request/response encoding=UTF-8/UTF-8
resource /WEB-INF/web.xml exists=true
resource /WEB-INF/../secret exists=false
request attribute who=request
session count=2 (new=false)
application visits=2
request attribute who=request
session count=1 (new=true)
application visits=3

The session count belongs to the cookie jar: the same client sees 2, a client without the cookie starts again at 1. The application count belongs to the context and keeps growing across clients. The feed.rss MIME type comes from the <mime-mapping> in the example’s web.xml, and the traversal attempt in the last line is refused: the path /WEB-INF/../secret yields null. Treat any path that includes user input as hostile and never pass it to getResource without checking it against an allowlist.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — Chapter 4, Servlet Context

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 4.5 Context Attributes

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 4.6 Resources

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — ServletContext

Sessions

HTTP is stateless, so the container associates requests of one client through a session id. The HttpSession interface hides the mechanism. Cookies are the mechanism every container must support, URL rewriting is the fallback, and an SSL session id is a third, rarely used option.

Table 13. Session tracking mechanisms (specification chapter 7)
Mechanism How it works Notes

Cookie

The container sends a cookie named JSESSIONID (renamable with <cookie-config><name>) and the client returns it on every request

Required of every container. Configure HttpOnly, Secure, path and extra attributes such as SameSite with <cookie-config> or SessionCookieConfig

URL rewriting

The id is appended to the path as ;jsessionid=... by response.encodeURL and encodeRedirectURL

Exposes the id in logs, bookmarks, Referer headers and the address bar; the specification itself says not to use it where cookies or SSL sessions are available

SSL session

The TLS session identifies the client

Container specific and rarely used

The session lifecycle is: created lazily by request.getSession() (or getSession(true)); looked up without creating by getSession(false), which returns null when there is none; replaced on privilege change with changeSessionId(); ended by invalidate() or by the idle timeout. A session is new until the client has returned the cookie, so the first request is the only one on which isNew() is true, and a servlet must work when the client never joins the session.

Timeouts have two scales: ServletContext.setSessionTimeout and <session-timeout> use minutes, while HttpSession.setMaxInactiveInterval uses seconds, and a zero or negative value means the session never expires.

The Cart class stores the books a visitor picked, and the CartServlet exercises the API:

A session attribute: Serializable, and told when it is bound
public class Cart implements Serializable, HttpSessionBindingListener {
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    private final List<Long> bookIds = new ArrayList<>();

    public synchronized void add(long id) {
        bookIds.add(id);
    }

    public synchronized List<Long> ids() {
        return List.copyOf(bookIds);
    }

    @Override
    public void valueBound(HttpSessionBindingEvent event) {
        EventLog.of(event.getSession().getServletContext()).add("Cart bound as " + event.getName());
    }

    @Override
    public void valueUnbound(HttpSessionBindingEvent event) {
        EventLog.of(event.getSession().getServletContext()).add("Cart unbound from " + event.getName());
    }
}

Objects stored in a session follow a few rules that come from the container, not from the language. They should be small and Serializable (the container may persist or replicate the session; Tomcat’s standard manager preserves sessions across restarts when its pathname attribute is set), thread-safe or guarded, because the same session can serve two requests at once, and well-behaved JavaBeans (public no-argument constructor, getXxx/isXxx/setXxx accessors) when a JSP is going to read them through EL. An object that needs to know when it joins or leaves a session implements HttpSessionBindingListener, as Cart does; one that holds non-serializable resources implements HttpSessionActivationListener to drop and re-acquire them around passivation. The bean conventions themselves are covered by Standard Actions & JavaBeans.

Creating, rotating, expiring and invalidating a session
@WebServlet("/cart")
public class CartServlet extends HttpServlet {

    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        HttpSession session = req.getSession();
        Cart cart = (Cart) session.getAttribute("cart");
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        PrintWriter out = resp.getWriter();
        out.println("new=" + session.isNew() + " idFromCookie=" + req.isRequestedSessionIdFromCookie()
                + " idFromURL=" + req.isRequestedSessionIdFromURL() + " valid=" + req.isRequestedSessionIdValid());
        out.println("maxInactiveInterval(s)=" + session.getMaxInactiveInterval());
        out.println("cart=" + (cart == null ? "empty" : cart.ids()));
        out.println("encodeURL=" + resp.encodeURL(req.getContextPath() + "/cart"));
        out.println("encodeRedirectURL=" + resp.encodeRedirectURL(req.getContextPath() + "/books"));
    }

    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        String action = String.valueOf(req.getParameter("action"));
        HttpSession session = req.getSession();
        switch (action) {
            case "add" -> {
                Cart cart = (Cart) session.getAttribute("cart");
                if (cart == null) {
                    cart = new Cart();
                    session.setAttribute("cart", cart);
                }
                cart.add(Long.parseLong(req.getParameter("book")));
            }
            case "rotate" -> req.changeSessionId();       // new id, same attributes: do it after any privilege change
            case "timeout" -> session.setMaxInactiveInterval(Integer.parseInt(req.getParameter("seconds")));
            case "logout" -> session.invalidate();         // listeners run, attributes are unbound
            default -> {
                resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST, "unknown action");
                return;
            }
        }
        resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/cart", HttpServletResponse.SC_SEE_OTHER);
    }
}
J=jar; B=http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet
curl -s -c $J -b $J $B/cart
curl -si -c $J -b $J -d 'action=add&book=1' $B/cart | head -3
curl -s -c $J -b $J -d 'action=add&book=3' -L $B/cart | sed -n 3p
curl -s -c $J -b $J -d 'action=rotate' -L $B/cart | sed -n 1,3p
curl -s -c $J -b $J -d 'action=timeout&seconds=120' -L $B/cart | sed -n 2p
curl -s -c $J -b $J -d 'action=logout' -L $B/cart | head -4
new=false idFromCookie=true idFromURL=false valid=true
maxInactiveInterval(s)=1800
cart=empty
encodeURL=/g2-servlet/cart
encodeRedirectURL=/g2-servlet/books
HTTP/1.1 303
Location: /g2-servlet/cart
Content-Length: 0
new=false idFromCookie=true idFromURL=false valid=true
maxInactiveInterval(s)=1800
cart=[1, 3]
new=false idFromCookie=true idFromURL=false valid=true
maxInactiveInterval(s)=1800
cart=[1, 3]
maxInactiveInterval(s)=120
new=true idFromCookie=true idFromURL=false valid=false
maxInactiveInterval(s)=1800
cart=empty
encodeURL=/g2-servlet/cart

The session id after rotate ends in a different four characters (...0D4E before, ...AD5F after) while the cart keeps its content: changeSessionId() swaps the identifier and keeps the attributes. After logout, the browser still presents the old cookie, so idFromCookie=true and valid=false tell the servlet that the id it was given is dead, and a fresh, empty session replaced it. Every state change is a POST answered by a 303 redirect.

The listeners of the example record what the container did (an excerpt of the /log trace, the listener section shows the code):

sessionCreated, active=4
Cart bound as cart
session attribute added: cart
sessionIdChanged (old id ends ...0D4E)
sessionDestroyed, active=3
session attribute removed: count
Cart unbound from cart
session attribute removed: cart

sessionIdChanged fires when changeSessionId() runs, and invalidate() produces sessionDestroyed and unbinds every attribute, calling valueUnbound on Cart.
