Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 7.5 Session Timeouts

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — HttpServletRequest.changeSessionId()

Source: Apache Tomcat 11 — The Manager Component

Session Security and Configuration

Four settings decide whether session handling is safe, and web.xml expresses all of them:

web.xml: timeout, cookie attributes and tracking mode
<session-config>
  <session-timeout>30</session-timeout>
  <cookie-config>
    <http-only>true</http-only>
    <attribute>
      <attribute-name>SameSite</attribute-name>
      <attribute-value>Lax</attribute-value>
    </attribute>
  </cookie-config>
  <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode>
</session-config>
Table 14. Session hardening checklist
Risk Defence in the servlet API

Session fixation: an attacker plants a known id, the victim logs in

Call request.changeSessionId() (or invalidate and create a new session) at the moment of login; LoginServlet of the example does, and the sessionIdChanged event confirms it

Session id in the URL

Restrict tracking to cookies with <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode>. Without it, the example showed ;jsessionid=... on the first response, see below

Cookie theft by script

<http-only>true</http-only>. The example sets it, and the Set-Cookie lines above show HttpOnly

Cookie sent on the wire in clear text or cross-site

<secure>true</secure> when the site is served over HTTPS (it is left off in the example, which runs on plain HTTP), plus SameSite

Idle sessions that never die

<session-timeout> in minutes; zero or negative means never expires

Non-serializable attributes in a clustered or persistent store

distributable applications must store only Serializable objects, or the container throws IllegalArgumentException

Using a session outside a request (WebSocket, background threads)

New in 6.1: HttpSession.getAccessor() returns an HttpSession.Accessor whose access(Consumer) runs a callback with the session, so you never keep a stale HttpSession reference

To see URL rewriting, the same WAR was deployed a second time without the <tracking-mode> element, and a client that does not yet hold a cookie asked for /cart:

curl -si http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet-var/cart | grep -i 'set-cookie\|encode'
Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=F669A335...; Path=/g2-servlet-var; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
encodeURL=/g2-servlet-var/cart;jsessionid=F669A335...
encodeRedirectURL=/g2-servlet-var/books;jsessionid=F669A335...

Until the container sees the cookie come back it cannot know that the client accepts cookies, so it makes encodeURL add the id to every link of that first page. The id then appears in the HTML, in any Referer header and in server logs. On the second request, with the cookie, encodeURL returned the plain path. With <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode> (the g2-servlet deployment) the rewriting never happens, which is the right choice for any site that does not need to serve cookieless clients.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 7.1.3 URL Rewriting

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — HttpSession.getAccessor()

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — SessionCookieConfig

Source: OWASP — Session Management Cheat Sheet

Cookies

A cookie is a name and value that the server asks the client to store and return. HttpServletResponse.addCookie emits a Set-Cookie header, HttpServletRequest.getCookies() reads the Cookie header and returns null when there is none. A browser sends back only the name and value, never the attributes, so getCookies() objects have no path, age or HttpOnly flag that you could inspect.

Servlet 6.0 moved the Cookie class from RFC 2109 to RFC 6265 and introduced generic attributes (issue 175): any attribute can be set with setAttribute(name, value), which is how SameSite and Partitioned are written, and 6.1 clarified valueless attributes such as HttpOnly, Secure and Partitioned (issue 571). setComment and setVersion are deprecated for removal because RFC 6265 no longer has them.

Table 15. Cookie attributes
Attribute API Meaning

Path

setPath

URL prefix that receives the cookie; default is the request path of the response, so set it explicitly (the context path)

Domain

setDomain

Host scope; leave it unset for a host-only cookie, which is the safest

Max-Age / Expires

setMaxAge(seconds)

Positive: persistent for that long. Negative (default): browser session only. Zero: delete (use the same name and path)

HttpOnly

setHttpOnly(true)

Hidden from JavaScript

Secure

setSecure(true)

Sent only over HTTPS

SameSite

setAttribute("SameSite", "Lax")

Strict, Lax or None (None also requires Secure) controls cross-site sending, a CSRF mitigation, not a replacement for a token

Partitioned

setAttribute("Partitioned", "")

Opts the cookie into partitioned third-party storage; an empty value writes the bare attribute
Setting, reading and clearing a preference cookie
@WebServlet("/prefs")
public class PrefsServlet extends HttpServlet {

    private static final Set<String> THEMES = Set.of("light", "dark");

    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        String theme = req.getParameter("theme");
        if (theme != null) {
            if (!THEMES.contains(theme)) {                     // never copy raw input into a cookie value
                resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST, "unknown theme");
                return;
            }
            Cookie cookie = new Cookie("theme", theme);
            cookie.setPath(req.getContextPath().isEmpty() ? "/" : req.getContextPath());
            cookie.setMaxAge(30 * 24 * 60 * 60);                // seconds; -1 = browser session, 0 = delete
            cookie.setHttpOnly(true);
            cookie.setSecure(req.isSecure());                   // Secure only makes sense over HTTPS
            cookie.setAttribute("SameSite", "Lax");              // Servlet 6.0: generic cookie attributes
            if ("1".equals(req.getParameter("partitioned"))) {
                cookie.setAttribute("Partitioned", "");          // attribute without a value
            }
            resp.addCookie(cookie);
            resp.getWriter().println("theme cookie set to " + theme);
        } else if ("1".equals(req.getParameter("clear"))) {
            Cookie cookie = new Cookie("theme", "");
            cookie.setPath(req.getContextPath().isEmpty() ? "/" : req.getContextPath());
            cookie.setMaxAge(0);                               // same name and path, or the browser keeps the old one
            resp.addCookie(cookie);
            resp.getWriter().println("theme cookie cleared");
        } else {
            Cookie[] cookies = req.getCookies();               // null when the request has no Cookie header
            String current = "none";
            if (cookies != null) {
                for (Cookie c : cookies) {
                    if (c.getName().equals("theme")) {
                        current = c.getValue();
                    }
                }
            }
            resp.getWriter().println("theme=" + current + " (browsers send only name and value back)");
        }
    }
}
curl -si 'http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/prefs?theme=dark' | grep -i set-cookie
curl -si 'http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/prefs?theme=dark&partitioned=1' | grep -i set-cookie
curl -s  -H 'Cookie: theme=dark; JSESSIONID=x' http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/prefs
curl -si 'http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/prefs?theme=%3Cscript%3E' | head -1
curl -si 'http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/prefs?clear=1' | grep -i set-cookie
Set-Cookie: theme=dark; Expires=Sat, 07 Nov 2026 10:24:32 GMT; Max-Age=2592000; Path=/g2-servlet; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Set-Cookie: theme=dark; Expires=Sat, 07 Nov 2026 10:24:32 GMT; Max-Age=2592000; Path=/g2-servlet; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Partitioned
theme=dark (browsers send only name and value back)
HTTP/1.1 400
Set-Cookie: theme=; Expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:10 GMT; Path=/g2-servlet

The first two lines show the SameSite and Partitioned attributes written exactly as the Javadoc table says. The value is validated against an allowlist before it reaches Set-Cookie, because cookie values built from request input are a header-injection and session-poisoning vector. The last line is how a cookie is deleted: same name and path, expiry in the past. The Secure flag is false in the example only because the scratch Tomcat speaks plain HTTP; on a real site always keep it on, and prefer server-side sessions for anything that identifies a user.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — Cookie.setAttribute(String, String)

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 3.10 Cookies

Source: RFC 6265 — HTTP State Management Mechanism

Filters, Wrappers and the Filter Chain

A filter is an object that intercepts requests to a servlet, a JSP or a static file, and responses on the way back. It can inspect or reject the request, wrap the request or response to change what later components see, and post-process the response. Authentication, logging, compression, character-encoding fixes, CORS headers and page layout (SiteMesh) are all filters, and so is the Struts 2 entry point, StrutsPrepareAndExecuteFilter (see Architecture & Request Lifecycle).

Table 16. The Filter contract
Member Rule

init(FilterConfig)

Called once per declaration before the first request; FilterConfig gives init parameters and the ServletContext. Throwing UnavailableException marks the filter unusable

doFilter(request, response, chain)

Called for every matching request, on the same thread as the servlet. Calls chain.doFilter(request, response) to continue, with the originals or with wrappers, or does not call it to block the request and write the response itself

destroy()

Called once when the filter is removed from service

One instance

One instance per <filter> declaration, shared by all threads, like a servlet. Declaring the same class twice creates two instances

Declaring and Ordering Filters

A filter is declared with @WebFilter or a <filter> element, and attached with <filter-mapping> to URL patterns or servlet names. The order of the chain is defined by the specification (section 6.2.4): first all <url-pattern> mappings that match the request, in the order they appear in web.xml, then all <servlet-name> mappings that match, in the order they appear. The last filter calls the servlet. The order of filters declared only by annotations is unspecified, so a chain whose order matters needs web.xml (or programmatic registration, where isMatchAfter controls the position).

The Bookshelf declares three instances of one timing filter, all with <async-supported>, in this order: a mapping by servlet name (written first), then outer and inner for /*:

A pass-through filter: code before and after chain.doFilter
public class TimingFilter implements Filter {
    private ServletContext ctx;
    private String label;

    @Override
    public void init(FilterConfig config) {
        ctx = config.getServletContext();
        label = config.getInitParameter("label");
    }

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest request, ServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        HttpServletRequest req = (HttpServletRequest) request;
        boolean trace = req.getHeader("X-Trace") != null;
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        if (trace) {
            EventLog.of(ctx).add(label + " before " + req.getDispatcherType() + " " + req.getRequestURI());
        }
        try {
            chain.doFilter(request, response);               // everything after this line runs on the way back
        } finally {
            if (trace) {
                EventLog.of(ctx).add(label + " after (" + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1000 + " us)");
            }
        }
    }
}
web.xml: a filter declaration (the others differ only by name and label)
<filter>
  <filter-name>by-servlet-name</filter-name>
  <filter-class>org.example.bookshelf.TimingFilter</filter-class>
  <async-supported>true</async-supported>
  <init-param><param-name>label</param-name><param-value>by-servlet-name</param-value></init-param>
</filter>

The full list of mappings, in declared order, is:

web.xml: the filter-mapping elements
<!-- Declared first, but matched by servlet name, so it runs after every url-pattern match. -->
<filter-mapping>
  <filter-name>by-servlet-name</filter-name>
  <servlet-name>fragment</servlet-name>
  <dispatcher>REQUEST</dispatcher>
  <dispatcher>FORWARD</dispatcher>
</filter-mapping>
<filter-mapping>
  <filter-name>outer</filter-name>
  <url-pattern>/*</url-pattern>
</filter-mapping>
<filter-mapping>
  <filter-name>inner</filter-name>
  <url-pattern>/*</url-pattern>
</filter-mapping>
<filter-mapping>
  <filter-name>trim</filter-name>
  <url-pattern>/search</url-pattern>
</filter-mapping>
<filter-mapping>
  <filter-name>footer</filter-name>
  <url-pattern>/WEB-INF/views/*</url-pattern>
  <dispatcher>FORWARD</dispatcher>
</filter-mapping>

A request that carries the header X-Trace makes the filters write to the trace, which /log shows:

curl -s -H 'X-Trace: 1' http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/fragment/x -o /dev/null
curl -s http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/log
outer before REQUEST /g2-servlet/fragment/x
inner before REQUEST /g2-servlet/fragment/x
DispatchTrace saw REQUEST /g2-servlet/fragment/x
by-servlet-name before REQUEST /g2-servlet/fragment/x
by-servlet-name after (160 us)
inner after (313 us)
outer after (328 us)

The picture matches the figure below: outer and inner (url-pattern mappings, in file order) run before the filter that was declared first but matches by servlet name, and the code after chain.doFilter runs in reverse. DispatchTraceFilter is declared by annotation only, so its position relative to the XML-declared filters is the container’s choice; in Tomcat 11 it ran after the XML url-pattern filters, but the specification does not promise that.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 6.2.4 Configuration of Filters in a Web Application

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 6.2.1 Filter Lifecycle

Dispatcher Types: Why a Filter Does Not Run on a Forward

A <filter-mapping> without <dispatcher> elements applies to REQUEST only. A filter that must also see forwards, includes, error pages or asynchronous dispatches names them explicitly; with annotations the attribute is dispatcherTypes.

Table 17. The dispatcher types of a filter mapping (specification 6.2.5)
Value When the filter runs

REQUEST

The request comes straight from the client. This is the default when no <dispatcher> is written

FORWARD

The request is processed under a RequestDispatcher.forward() to the matching resource

INCLUDE

Under a RequestDispatcher.include() to the matching resource

ERROR

The resource is an error page invoked by the error page mechanism

ASYNC

Under an AsyncContext.dispatch call

The annotated DispatchTraceFilter lists all of them for the paths of the next examples:

Observing every dispatcher type
@WebFilter(urlPatterns = {"/dispatch", "/fragment/*", "/errors/*", "/boom"},
        dispatcherTypes = {DispatcherType.REQUEST, DispatcherType.FORWARD, DispatcherType.INCLUDE, DispatcherType.ERROR})
public class DispatchTraceFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest request, ServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        HttpServletRequest req = (HttpServletRequest) request;
        if (req.getHeader("X-Trace") != null) {
            EventLog.of(req.getServletContext()).add("DispatchTrace saw " + req.getDispatcherType() + " "
                    + req.getRequestURI());
        }
        chain.doFilter(request, response);
    }
}

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 6.2.5 Filters and the RequestDispatcher

Wrapping the Request

HttpServletRequestWrapper and HttpServletResponseWrapper implement the decorator pattern: a filter creates a subclass that overrides a few methods, passes the wrapper to chain.doFilter, and every servlet, JSP and later filter sees the modified behaviour without being aware of it. The container must pass the wrapper itself (or a wrapper of it) on to the next component (section 6.2.2).

The TrimFilter below wraps the request so that every parameter value reaches the servlet already trimmed. A wrapper must override all the accessors that expose the same data (getParameter, getParameterValues, getParameterMap, and getParameterNames uses the unchanged keys), or code that uses the one you forgot sees the raw value.

A request wrapper that trims parameters
public class TrimFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest request, ServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        chain.doFilter(new TrimmedRequest((HttpServletRequest) request), response);
    }

    static final class TrimmedRequest extends HttpServletRequestWrapper {
        TrimmedRequest(HttpServletRequest request) {
            super(request);
        }

        @Override
        public String getParameter(String name) {
            String value = super.getParameter(name);
            return value == null ? null : value.strip();
        }

        @Override
        public String[] getParameterValues(String name) {
            String[] values = super.getParameterValues(name);
            return values == null ? null : Arrays.stream(values).map(String::strip).toArray(String[]::new);
        }

        @Override
        public Map<String, String[]> getParameterMap() {   // override all accessors, or the filter has holes
            return super.getParameterMap().entrySet().stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(
                    Map.Entry::getKey, e -> Arrays.stream(e.getValue()).map(String::strip).toArray(String[]::new)));
        }
    }
}

It is mapped only to /search and produced the trimmed title=Dune result shown in the request section, for a query string that contained %20Dune%20.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 6.2.2 Wrapping Requests and Responses

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — HttpServletRequestWrapper

Wrapping the Response and Why FORWARD Matters

A response wrapper captures the output of the rest of the chain so the filter can change it before it reaches the client: compress it, rewrite links, decorate it with a layout. The FooterFilter buffers a page in a CharArrayWriter and appends an HTML comment after the content of every text/html response:

A response wrapper that appends a footer to HTML
public class FooterFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest request, ServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        CapturingResponse wrapper = new CapturingResponse((HttpServletResponse) response);
        chain.doFilter(request, wrapper);
        String type = wrapper.getContentType();
        if (wrapper.captured() != null && type != null && type.startsWith("text/html")) {
            String html = wrapper.captured().toString();
            response.getWriter().write(html);
            response.getWriter().write("<!-- rendered by Bookshelf -->\n");
        } else if (wrapper.captured() != null) {
            response.getWriter().write(wrapper.captured().toString());
        }
    }

    static final class CapturingResponse extends HttpServletResponseWrapper {
        private CharArrayWriter buffer;
        private PrintWriter writer;

        CapturingResponse(HttpServletResponse response) {
            super(response);
        }

        @Override
        public PrintWriter getWriter() {
            if (writer == null) {
                buffer = new CharArrayWriter();
                writer = new PrintWriter(buffer);
            }
            return writer;
        }

        CharArrayWriter captured() {
            if (writer != null) {
                writer.flush();
            }
            return buffer;
        }
    }
}

The page it decorates is the output of a JSP, and the JSP is reached by a forward from BookServlet. The first version of the mapping used the default REQUEST dispatcher on /books/*, and the result was an empty page:

HTTP/1.1 200
Content-Type: text/html;charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 0

The filter had captured the HTML (149 characters in the debug run), but it was written to a response that Tomcat had already finished. The specification requires the container to send, commit and close the response before forward returns, and Tomcat does that to the real response, not to the wrapper, so code that runs after chain.doFilter in a REQUEST filter is too late. The fix is to run the filter around the forwarded resource. The final mapping applies the filter to the JSP views under WEB-INF and only for the FORWARD dispatcher, as shown in the mapping list above (/WEB-INF/views/*, <dispatcher>FORWARD</dispatcher>), and the page now ends with the footer:

curl -si http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/books/1
HTTP/1.1 200
Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=5E99CAFF...; Path=/g2-servlet; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Content-Type: text/html;charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 178

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h1>Dune</h1>
<p>by Frank Herbert, 1965</p>
<p><a href="/g2-servlet/books">Back to the shelf</a></p>
</body>
</html>
<!-- rendered by Bookshelf -->

Layout frameworks such as SiteMesh use exactly this arrangement, and the Tiles & Page Layouts page of this section comes back to it. Two details of the wrapper above are worth copying into any real one: it implements only getWriter (a page that calls getOutputStream needs a second path), and it never sets Content-Length, because the length changes after the filter appends text.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 9.4 The Forward Method

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — HttpServletResponseWrapper

A Filter That Blocks: Authentication and Authorization

A filter that does not call chain.doFilter ends the request. The AdminFilter protects /admin/* and the LoginServlet shows the safe login sequence (validate, rotate the session id, store the identity, redirect):

A filter that blocks anonymous requests
@WebFilter("/admin/*")
public class AdminFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest request, ServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        HttpServletRequest req = (HttpServletRequest) request;
        HttpServletResponse resp = (HttpServletResponse) response;
        HttpSession session = req.getSession(false);
        if (session == null || session.getAttribute("user") == null) {
            resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED, "Sign in first");
            return;
        }
        chain.doFilter(request, response);
    }
}
Login: rotate the session id first
@WebServlet("/login")
public class LoginServlet extends HttpServlet {
    private static final Pattern USER = Pattern.compile("[a-z]{3,20}");

    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        String user = req.getParameter("user");
        if (user == null || !USER.matcher(user).matches()) {
            resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST);
            return;
        }
        req.getSession();
        req.changeSessionId();                                  // new id at the moment of login: no session fixation
        req.getSession().setAttribute("user", user);
        resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/admin/stats", HttpServletResponse.SC_SEE_OTHER);
    }
}
The protected resource
@WebServlet("/admin/stats")
public class AdminServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        resp.getWriter().println("admin area for " + req.getSession().getAttribute("user")
                + ", active sessions=" + getServletContext().getAttribute("activeSessions"));
    }
}
B=http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet; J=jar
curl -si $B/admin/stats | head -1
curl -si -c $J -b $J -d 'user=ROOT!' $B/login | head -1
curl -si -c $J -b $J -d 'user=alice' $B/login | sed -n '1p;3p'
curl -s  -c $J -b $J $B/admin/stats
HTTP/1.1 401
HTTP/1.1 400
HTTP/1.1 303
Location: /g2-servlet/admin/stats
admin area for alice, active sessions=1

A role filter has the same shape: after the identity check it compares a stored role set, or request.isUserInRole(role) when the container authenticates, and answers 403 instead of 401. A logging or auditing filter is the TimingFilter shape, and the content-rewriting filter is the FooterFilter above.

This identity check is a teaching stub. Real applications use container-managed authentication (<login-config>, <security-constraint>, HttpServletRequest.login), the Jakarta Security API or Spring Security, which handle credentials, password storage and role mapping; Security covers the container mechanisms (Servlet chapter 13).

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 6.1 What is a Filter

Source: OWASP — Session fixation

Listeners: Application, Session and Request Events

Listeners are classes that the container calls when something happens in the web application. They are how an application starts and stops its own resources, counts sessions, and reacts to attribute changes.

Table 18. The listener interfaces (specification chapter 11)
Interface Events Typical use

ServletContextListener

contextInitialized, contextDestroyed

Load configuration and seed data, create thread pools and clients, register servlets and filters programmatically; stop them on shutdown

ServletContextAttributeListener

attribute added, removed, replaced on the context

Audit or react to application-scope changes

HttpSessionListener

sessionCreated, sessionDestroyed

Count active users, release per-user resources

HttpSessionAttributeListener

attribute added, removed, replaced on a session

Track what is stored in sessions

HttpSessionIdListener

sessionIdChanged

Audit changeSessionId() calls

HttpSessionActivationListener

sessionWillPassivate, sessionDidActivate

Implemented by a session attribute, to release and re-acquire non-serializable resources when a clustered or persistent container moves the session (for example a Tomcat manager configured to keep sessions across restarts)

HttpSessionBindingListener

valueBound, valueUnbound

Implemented by the attribute object itself (Cart in the example)

ServletRequestListener

requestInitialized, requestDestroyed

Per-request set-up and tear-down, for example thread-local cleanup

ServletRequestAttributeListener

attribute added, removed, replaced on a request

Debugging and auditing

AsyncListener

onStartAsync, onComplete, onTimeout, onError

Registered on an AsyncContext; clean up when an async cycle ends

Registration is by @WebListener, by a <listener> element, or programmatically with ServletContext.addListener. Listener instances are created once per declaration, so they follow the same thread-safety rules as servlets. The order in which the container calls listeners of the same type is the order of declaration in web.xml; annotation-declared ones are not ordered. A listener that throws during contextInitialized prevents the application from starting.

The AppListener of the example loads the catalogue from WEB-INF at startup, publishes the shared objects as context attributes, and registers a servlet programmatically. The SessionTracker counts sessions:

A context listener: seed data, shared objects and a programmatic servlet
@WebListener
public class AppListener implements ServletContextListener, ServletContextAttributeListener {

    @Override
    public void contextInitialized(ServletContextEvent event) {
        ServletContext ctx = event.getServletContext();
        EventLog log = new EventLog();
        ctx.setAttribute(EventLog.ATTRIBUTE, log);

        Catalogue catalogue = new Catalogue();
        try (InputStream in = ctx.getResourceAsStream("/WEB-INF/catalogue.csv");
             BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(in, StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {
            reader.lines().skip(1).map(l -> l.split(";")).forEach(
                    f -> catalogue.add(f[0], f[1], Integer.parseInt(f[2])));
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new UncheckedIOException(e);
        }
        ctx.setAttribute(Catalogue.ATTRIBUTE, catalogue);
        ctx.setAttribute("visits", new AtomicInteger());
        ctx.setAttribute("activeSessions", new AtomicInteger());

        // Programmatic registration is allowed here because this listener is annotated (not added programmatically).
        ctx.addServlet("ping", PingServlet.class).addMapping("/ping");
        log.add("initializer found filters: " + ctx.getAttribute("filtersFound"));
        log.add("contextInitialized: " + catalogue.all().size() + " books, title=" + ctx.getInitParameter("catalogue.title"));
    }

    @Override
    public void contextDestroyed(ServletContextEvent event) {
        EventLog.of(event.getServletContext()).add("contextDestroyed");
    }

    @Override
    public void attributeAdded(ServletContextAttributeEvent event) {
        if (!"eventLog".equals(event.getName())) {
            EventLog.of(event.getServletContext()).add("context attribute added: " + event.getName());
        }
    }
}
Session, attribute and id-change events
@WebListener
public class SessionTracker implements HttpSessionListener, HttpSessionAttributeListener, HttpSessionIdListener {

    private static AtomicInteger active(HttpSessionEvent e) {
        return (AtomicInteger) e.getSession().getServletContext().getAttribute("activeSessions");
    }

    @Override
    public void sessionCreated(HttpSessionEvent e) {
        int n = active(e).incrementAndGet();
        EventLog.of(e.getSession().getServletContext()).add("sessionCreated, active=" + n);
    }

    @Override
    public void sessionDestroyed(HttpSessionEvent e) {
        int n = active(e).decrementAndGet();
        EventLog.of(e.getSession().getServletContext()).add("sessionDestroyed, active=" + n);
    }

    @Override
    public void sessionIdChanged(HttpSessionEvent e, String oldSessionId) {
        EventLog.of(e.getSession().getServletContext()).add("sessionIdChanged (old id ends ..."
                + oldSessionId.substring(oldSessionId.length() - 4) + ")");
    }

    @Override
    public void attributeAdded(HttpSessionBindingEvent e) {
        EventLog.of(e.getSession().getServletContext()).add("session attribute added: " + e.getName());
    }

    @Override
    public void attributeRemoved(HttpSessionBindingEvent e) {
        EventLog.of(e.getSession().getServletContext()).add("session attribute removed: " + e.getName());
    }
}
The servlet that AppListener registers without annotation or web.xml
public class PingServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        resp.getWriter().println("pong from " + getServletName());
    }
}

The startup trace and the programmatic servlet:

curl -s http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/log | head -5
curl -s http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/ping
context attribute added: catalogue
context attribute added: visits
context attribute added: activeSessions
contextInitialized: 3 books, title=Bookshelf
LifecycleServlet.init, instance 1266317426
pong from ping

The order of the lines is informative. The ServletContextAttributeListener events for catalogue, visits and activeSessions come before the "contextInitialized" line, because the attributes are added inside contextInitialized and the log line is written at its end. LifecycleServlet.init runs afterwards because loadOnStartup servlets are initialized once all context listeners have run. The /ping servlet, which has no entry anywhere in the WAR, answers because addServlet(...).addMapping("/ping") ran during initialization; the spec allows the call because AppListener is declared in the application (annotated or in web.xml), whereas a listener that was itself added programmatically may not register servlets. Registration after initialization throws IllegalStateException.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 11.2.1 Event Types and Listener Interfaces

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 11.3 Listener Class Configuration

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 4.4.1 Programmatically Adding and Configuring Servlets

Annotations Versus web.xml

Since Servlet 3.0 a web application does not need a web.xml at all: servlets, filters, listeners and multipart settings can be declared on the classes. The two mechanisms describe the same metadata, and the specification defines how they combine.

Table 19. Annotation and deployment-descriptor equivalents
Annotation web.xml element Notes

@WebServlet

<servlet> and <servlet-mapping>

Needs value or urlPatterns (not both). The default name is the fully qualified class name. loadOnStartup, initParams, asyncSupported are attributes. The class must extend HttpServlet

@WebFilter

<filter> and <filter-mapping>

urlPatterns, servletNames, dispatcherTypes, initParams, asyncSupported. No ordering attribute: use web.xml

@WebListener

<listener>

Listener type is detected from the interfaces the class implements

@WebInitParam

<init-param>

Used inside initParams

@MultipartConfig

<multipart-config>

Enables Part handling for a servlet

@ServletSecurity, @HttpConstraint

<security-constraint>

Covered by Security

@HandlesTypes

(none)

Only for a ServletContainerInitializer; always processed, even when metadata-complete is true

The merging rules (section 8.2.3) fit in five sentences. Annotations are read only from classes in WEB-INF/classes and in JARs in WEB-INF/lib. The web.xml of the application has the highest precedence and overrides conflicting values of annotations and fragments. metadata-complete="true" on the web-app element turns off annotation scanning and fragment processing. A servlet declared both ways under the same name is one servlet with the XML values winning, while the same class declared under different names is two instances, as the MappingServlet example does on purpose. When the order of filters, servlets (by load-on-startup) or listeners matters, it must come from web.xml; listeners of one kind are called in declaration order, and contextDestroyed, requestDestroyed and sessionDestroyed in reverse order.

The 6.1 schema and the document header that the example uses are:

The Servlet 6.1 descriptor header
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<web-app xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee/web-app_6_1.xsd"
         version="6.1">

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 8.2.3 Assembling the Descriptor from web.xml, web-fragment.xml and Annotations

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 8.1.1 @WebServlet

Source: Jakarta EE — web-app_6_1.xsd

Pluggability: Fragments and ServletContainerInitializer

Frameworks plug into a web application without touching web.xml. A library JAR in WEB-INF/lib can carry a META-INF/web-fragment.xml that contributes servlets, filters and listeners (ordered with <ordering> or the application’s <absolute-ordering>), static resources under META-INF/resources, and a ServletContainerInitializer registered in META-INF/services/jakarta.servlet.ServletContainerInitializer. The container calls onStartup(Set<Class<?>>, ServletContext) before any listener, passing every class that matches the @HandlesTypes annotation of the initializer. This is how Spring’s SpringServletContainerInitializer, Jasper and Jakarta Faces start themselves, and why a JAR on the classpath can change the behaviour of an application.

The example has a tiny initializer, registered through the services file, that records which filters the container found:

A ServletContainerInitializer that reports the Filter classes it was handed
@HandlesTypes(Filter.class)
public class ScanInitializer implements ServletContainerInitializer {
    @Override
    public void onStartup(Set<Class<?>> classes, ServletContext ctx) {
        List<String> names = classes == null ? List.of()
                : classes.stream().map(Class::getSimpleName).sorted().toList();
        ctx.setAttribute("filtersFound", names);
    }
}
WEB-INF/classes/META-INF/services/jakarta.servlet.ServletContainerInitializer:
org.example.bookshelf.ScanInitializer
initializer found filters: [AdminFilter, DispatchTraceFilter, FooterFilter, TimingFilter, TrimFilter]
contextInitialized: 3 books, title=Bookshelf

The first line is written by AppListener from the attribute the initializer set: the initializer ran first and saw the five filter classes of the WAR, annotated or not.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 8.2 Pluggability

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 Javadoc — ServletContainerInitializer

RequestDispatcher: Forward, Include and Named Dispatch

A RequestDispatcher hands the current request to another resource inside the same container: a servlet, a JSP, a static file. It is the mechanism behind the Model 2 pattern (built out in MVC with Servlets & JSP): a controller servlet prepares the model as request attributes and forwards to a JSP that renders it (the BookServlet of this page does so). It comes from request.getRequestDispatcher(path) (the path may be relative to the current servlet), ServletContext.getRequestDispatcher(path) (must start with /) or ServletContext.getNamedDispatcher(name) (a servlet name from web.xml or @WebServlet(name=...)). A path can carry a query string, and the container merges the new parameters with the original ones, the new values first.

Table 20. forward, include and sendRedirect compared
forward include sendRedirect

What the client sees

one response, original URL

one response, original URL

a 3xx and a second request to a new URL

Request and attributes

same request; model attributes survive

same request; model attributes survive

lost (new request); use the session or a flash mechanism

Response handling

uncommitted output is discarded and the response is committed and closed when forward returns

the target appends to the output but cannot change status or headers (calls are ignored)

no body of its own

Path methods

describe the target

still describe the including request

not applicable

Request attributes added

jakarta.servlet.forward.* with the original path elements

jakarta.servlet.include.* with the target’s

none

Allowed when committed

throws IllegalStateException

yes

throws IllegalStateException

Typical use

controller to view

page fragments, headers and footers

after a state-changing POST

The DispatchServlet and FragmentServlet of the example exercise every variation. FragmentServlet prints what it sees:

The dispatch target: it prints the path elements and the forward and include attributes
@WebServlet(name = "fragment", urlPatterns = "/fragment/*")
public class FragmentServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        resp.setHeader("X-Ignored", "set-by-fragment");     // ignored when this servlet is being included
        PrintWriter out = resp.getWriter();
        out.println("-- fragment: dispatcher=" + req.getDispatcherType() + " uri=" + req.getRequestURI()
                + " servletPath=" + req.getServletPath() + " pathInfo=" + req.getPathInfo()
                + " query=" + req.getQueryString());
        for (String name : List.of(RequestDispatcher.FORWARD_REQUEST_URI, RequestDispatcher.FORWARD_QUERY_STRING,
                RequestDispatcher.FORWARD_MAPPING, RequestDispatcher.INCLUDE_REQUEST_URI,
                RequestDispatcher.INCLUDE_QUERY_STRING, RequestDispatcher.INCLUDE_SERVLET_PATH)) {
            Object value = req.getAttribute(name);
            out.println("   " + name + " = " + (value instanceof jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletMapping m
                    ? m.getMappingMatch() + ":" + m.getPattern() : value));
        }
        out.println("   from parameter=" + req.getParameter("from"));
    }
}
Forward, include, named dispatcher and misuse
@WebServlet("/dispatch")
public class DispatchServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws ServletException, IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        String mode = String.valueOf(req.getParameter("mode"));
        switch (mode) {
            case "forward" -> {
                resp.getWriter().println("this text is discarded: forward clears the uncommitted buffer");
                req.getRequestDispatcher("/fragment/view?from=forward").forward(req, resp);
            }
            case "include" -> {
                PrintWriter out = resp.getWriter();
                out.println("before include");
                req.getRequestDispatcher("/fragment/view?from=include").include(req, resp);
                out.println("after include, status=" + resp.getStatus() + " header X-Ignored=" + resp.getHeader("X-Ignored"));
            }
            case "named" -> getServletContext().getNamedDispatcher("fragment").forward(req, resp);
            case "forward-after-commit" -> {
                resp.getWriter().println("committed");
                resp.flushBuffer();
                try {
                    req.getRequestDispatcher("/fragment/view").forward(req, resp);
                } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
                    resp.getWriter().println("forward after commit -> IllegalStateException");
                }
            }
            case "missing" -> {
                RequestDispatcher d = req.getRequestDispatcher("/does/not/exist");
                resp.getWriter().println("dispatcher for an unknown path is never null here: " + (d != null));
            }
            default -> resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST, "modes: forward, include, named, forward-after-commit, missing");
        }
    }
}
B=http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet
curl -s "$B/dispatch?mode=forward&p=1"
curl -s "$B/dispatch?mode=include"
curl -s "$B/dispatch?mode=named&x=1"
curl -s "$B/dispatch?mode=forward-after-commit"
-- fragment: dispatcher=FORWARD uri=/g2-servlet/fragment/view servletPath=/fragment pathInfo=/view query=from=forward
   jakarta.servlet.forward.request_uri = /g2-servlet/dispatch
   jakarta.servlet.forward.query_string = mode=forward&p=1
   jakarta.servlet.forward.mapping = EXACT:/dispatch
   jakarta.servlet.include.request_uri = null
   jakarta.servlet.include.query_string = null
   jakarta.servlet.include.servlet_path = null
   from parameter=forward
before include
-- fragment: dispatcher=INCLUDE uri=/g2-servlet/dispatch servletPath=/dispatch pathInfo=null query=mode=include
   jakarta.servlet.forward.request_uri = null
   jakarta.servlet.forward.query_string = null
   jakarta.servlet.forward.mapping = null
   jakarta.servlet.include.request_uri = /g2-servlet/fragment/view
   jakarta.servlet.include.query_string = from=include
   jakarta.servlet.include.servlet_path = /fragment
   from parameter=include
after include, status=200 header X-Ignored=null
-- fragment: dispatcher=FORWARD uri=/g2-servlet/dispatch servletPath=/dispatch pathInfo=null query=mode=named&x=1
   jakarta.servlet.forward.request_uri = null
   ...
   from parameter=null
committed
forward after commit -> IllegalStateException

The four outputs show the differences in the table. In the forward, the path methods describe the target (/fragment/view), the original request is in the forward.* attributes, the text the dispatcher wrote before forwarding is gone, and from is forward, the new query parameter. In the include, the opposite holds: getRequestURI() is still /g2-servlet/dispatch, the target’s path is in the include.* attributes, and the header the fragment tried to set (X-Ignored) never arrived. A resource that must know its real path when it can be included therefore reads the attribute first and falls back to the method. In the named dispatch the target sees the original path and no forward attributes at all, because no path was used. Forwarding after a flush is rejected.

The filter trace of a forward and of an include (X-Trace header, outer/inner use the default REQUEST mapping):

forward:  outer before REQUEST /g2-servlet/dispatch
          inner before REQUEST /g2-servlet/dispatch
          DispatchTrace saw REQUEST /g2-servlet/dispatch
          DispatchTrace saw FORWARD /g2-servlet/fragment/view
          by-servlet-name before FORWARD /g2-servlet/fragment/view
          by-servlet-name after (188 us)
          inner after (399 us)
          outer after (414 us)
include:  outer before REQUEST /g2-servlet/dispatch
          inner before REQUEST /g2-servlet/dispatch
          DispatchTrace saw REQUEST /g2-servlet/dispatch
          DispatchTrace saw INCLUDE /g2-servlet/dispatch
          inner after (1336 us)
          outer after (1362 us)

outer and inner ran once, for the client request. DispatchTraceFilter, which lists all dispatcher types, saw the forward and the include, and the filter mapped by servlet name and for FORWARD joined only when the forward reached fragment. The include is not seen by by-servlet-name because that mapping lists only REQUEST and FORWARD. Note the URI printed for the include: it is the including request’s.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 9.4 The Forward Method

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 9.3 The Include Method

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 9.1 Obtaining a RequestDispatcher

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 9.4.2 Forwarded Request Parameters

URL Mapping Rules

The container maps a request to a servlet in two steps. It first picks the web application with the longest context path that matches the start of the URL. Within the application it removes the context path and any path parameters (such as ;jsessionid=...), decodes the rest as UTF-8, and applies these rules in order, stopping at the first match:

Table 21. The mapping algorithm (section 12.1) and the URL pattern forms (section 12.2)
Step Pattern form Rule

1

exact: a string such as /map/exact

The whole path equals the pattern

2

path prefix: /map/*

The longest prefix match, one directory at a time; the pattern matches /map, /map/ and everything below it

3

extension: *.report

The last segment ends in .report

4

default: /

The "default" servlet of the application (Tomcat’s DefaultServlet serves static files unless you replace it)

special

the empty string ""

Exactly the context root, with or without the trailing slash; the servlet path is the empty string

special

the implicit *.jsp

When the container has a JSP engine, *.jsp maps to it, unless the application defines its own *.jsp mapping

Matching is case sensitive. Patterns that mix wildcards (/WEB-INF/views/*.jsp) are invalid, and Tomcat refused to deploy the example when it contained one: the log said Invalid <url-pattern> [/WEB-INF/views/*.jsp] in servlet mapping. If the same pattern maps to two servlets in the effective configuration, deployment fails.

HttpServletRequest.getHttpServletMapping() (Servlet 4.0) reports how the match happened. MappingServlet prints it, and the WAR declares the class three times in web.xml (once per pattern), so three instances exist:

Reporting the mapping that selected the servlet
public class MappingServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        HttpServletMapping m = req.getHttpServletMapping();
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        PrintWriter out = resp.getWriter();
        out.println("servlet=" + getServletName() + " instance=" + System.identityHashCode(this));
        out.println("match=" + m.getMappingMatch() + " pattern='" + m.getPattern() + "' matchValue='" + m.getMatchValue() + "'");
        out.println("requestURI=" + req.getRequestURI());
        out.println("contextPath='" + req.getContextPath() + "' servletPath='" + req.getServletPath()
                + "' pathInfo=" + req.getPathInfo());
    }
}
web.xml: three declarations of MappingServlet and the first mapping (the others map /map/* and *.report)
<servlet>
  <servlet-name>mapping-exact</servlet-name>
  <servlet-class>org.example.bookshelf.MappingServlet</servlet-class>
</servlet>
<servlet>
  <servlet-name>mapping-prefix</servlet-name>
  <servlet-class>org.example.bookshelf.MappingServlet</servlet-class>
</servlet>
<servlet>
  <servlet-name>mapping-extension</servlet-name>
  <servlet-class>org.example.bookshelf.MappingServlet</servlet-class>
</servlet>
<servlet-mapping>
  <servlet-name>mapping-exact</servlet-name>
  <url-pattern>/map/exact</url-pattern>
</servlet-mapping>
B=http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet
curl -s $B/map/exact ; curl -s $B/map/a/b ; curl -s $B/reports/q1.report
servlet=mapping-exact instance=223862864
match=EXACT pattern='/map/exact' matchValue='map/exact'
requestURI=/g2-servlet/map/exact
contextPath='/g2-servlet' servletPath='/map/exact' pathInfo=null
servlet=mapping-prefix instance=1832380977
match=PATH pattern='/map/*' matchValue='a/b'
requestURI=/g2-servlet/map/a/b
contextPath='/g2-servlet' servletPath='/map' pathInfo=/a/b
servlet=mapping-extension instance=2010951165
match=EXTENSION pattern='*.report' matchValue='reports/q1'
requestURI=/g2-servlet/reports/q1.report
contextPath='/g2-servlet' servletPath='/reports/q1.report' pathInfo=null

The three servletPath and pathInfo pairs are the key to reading paths: for an exact or extension match the servlet path is the whole path and the path info is null; for a prefix match the servlet path is the prefix and the path info is the rest. getContextPath() + getServletPath() + getPathInfo() rebuilds the URI. A controller mapped to /books/* reads the id from the path info (/books/2 gives /2), as BookServlet does.

WAR Structure, WEB-INF and Welcome Files

A web application is a directory tree, usually packaged as a WAR (a JAR with the .war extension). The public part is the tree below the root; everything under WEB-INF is private to the container.

The layout of the example WAR (jar tf g2-servlet.war, abridged)
/                                  public: served as static files or mapped to servlets
├── hello.jsp                        a JSP in the public tree (reachable, implicit *.jsp mapping)
├── docs/index.html                  a directory with a welcome file
├── errors/readme.txt                a plain static file
├── META-INF/MANIFEST.MF
└── WEB-INF/                         never served to a client
    ├── web.xml                      the deployment descriptor
    ├── catalogue.csv                private data read with getResourceAsStream
    ├── views/books.jsp              JSP views, reachable only through a dispatcher
    ├── views/book.jsp
    ├── views/about.jsp
    ├── classes/org/example/bookshelf/*.class
    ├── classes/META-INF/services/jakarta.servlet.ServletContainerInitializer
    └── lib/jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl-api-3.0.2.jar, jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl-3.0.1.jar
Table 23. What lives where
Location Rule

Application root

Public static files and JSPs; a request for /docs/index.html is answered from here

WEB-INF/web.xml

The deployment descriptor, optional since Servlet 3.0

WEB-INF/classes

Compiled classes and resources on the application’s class path, found before JARs; annotations are scanned here

WEB-INF/lib/*.jar

Libraries, including JARs with fragments, TLDs and META-INF/resources; JARs are scanned for annotations

WEB-INF (anything else)

Private. A request for /WEB-INF/web.xml gives 404 even though the file exists, but a forward from a servlet may target it; this is why views belong here

META-INF

Metadata of the archive; META-INF/resources in a library JAR is served as if it were in the root

The Servlet API JAR

Not in WEB-INF/lib: the container provides it, and the Maven scope provided keeps it out of the WAR (the listing above has only the two JSTL JARs)

The test that confirmed the privacy of WEB-INF and the behaviour of directories and welcome files:

B=http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' $B/WEB-INF/web.xml
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' $B/WEB-INF/views/books.jsp
curl -si $B/docs | head -2
curl -s $B/docs/
404
404
HTTP/1.1 302
Location: /g2-servlet/docs/
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html><body><h1>Docs welcome page</h1></body></html>

A welcome file answers a request for a directory. The web.xml lists them in order:

web.xml: welcome files
<welcome-file-list>
  <welcome-file>index.html</welcome-file>
  <welcome-file>default.jsp</welcome-file>
</welcome-file-list>

For /docs (without the slash) the container redirects to /docs/, then appends index.html, finds a static file, and serves it. If no static file matches, it tries the names as servlet mappings (default.jsp), and if nothing matches, the container decides: a listing or a 404. Because the example maps the empty pattern to HomeServlet, the context root is answered by that servlet and not by a welcome file, a case where the explicit mapping wins.

Deployment to Tomcat is a copy: drop g2-servlet.war into webapps/ (the context path is the file name without .war), use the Manager application, or set unpackWARs/autoDeploy on the host. The Getting Started page of this section covers the Maven, Jetty and Docker routes. For the javax to jakarta change, Tomcat 10 and later do not run javax.servlet code; the Tomcat migration tool converts old WARs (see What’s Changed & Migration).

Error Pages

When a servlet calls sendError or lets an exception escape, the container renders an error response. The <error-page> element replaces the container’s default report with an application resource (the JSP side, with the errorPage attribute and isErrorPage, is in Error Handling; Struts maps exceptions to results instead, see Exception Handling and Global Results):

web.xml: error pages
<error-page>
  <error-code>404</error-code>
  <location>/errors/generic</location>
</error-page>
<error-page>
  <exception-type>java.sql.SQLException</exception-type>
  <location>/errors/database</location>
</error-page>
<error-page>
  <location>/errors/generic</location>
</error-page>

The matching rules (section 10.9.2) are:

  1. sendError(status): an <error-code> entry for that status.

  2. An exception that escapes: the <exception-type> entry whose class is the closest in the class hierarchy.

  3. If none matches and the exception is a ServletException, a second pass with getRootCause().

  4. Otherwise the default entry, an <error-page> without code and type.

  5. Otherwise the container’s own page, with status 500 for uncaught exceptions.

The error page is invoked by an ERROR dispatch that always uses the HTTP method GET, whatever the original method was, with the request path and attributes set as for a forward. Servlet 6.1 added jakarta.servlet.error.method for the original method and jakarta.servlet.error.query_string.

Table 25. The error request attributes (Table 10-1 plus the 6.1 additions)
Attribute Type Content

jakarta.servlet.error.status_code

Integer

The status code

jakarta.servlet.error.exception_type

Class

The exception class (kept for old code; the exception attribute is more useful)

jakarta.servlet.error.message

String

The message passed to sendError or the exception message

jakarta.servlet.error.exception

Throwable

The exception that escaped

jakarta.servlet.error.request_uri

String

The URI of the failing request

jakarta.servlet.error.query_string

String

6.1: the query string of the failing request

jakarta.servlet.error.servlet_name

String

The servlet that failed

jakarta.servlet.error.method

String

6.1: the original HTTP method

ErrorServlet prints them, and BoomServlet produces each kind of failure:

An error page: always GET, reads the error attributes
@WebServlet(name = "errors", urlPatterns = {"/errors/generic", "/errors/database"})
public class ErrorServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        Integer status = (Integer) req.getAttribute(RequestDispatcher.ERROR_STATUS_CODE);
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        if (status != null) {
            resp.setStatus(status);                         // an error page keeps the original status unless you set it
        }
        PrintWriter out = resp.getWriter();
        out.println("error page " + req.getServletPath() + " dispatcher=" + req.getDispatcherType()
                + " handled-as=" + req.getMethod());
        out.println("status=" + status);
        out.println("message=" + req.getAttribute(RequestDispatcher.ERROR_MESSAGE));
        out.println("exception_type=" + req.getAttribute(RequestDispatcher.ERROR_EXCEPTION_TYPE));
        out.println("exception=" + req.getAttribute(RequestDispatcher.ERROR_EXCEPTION));
        out.println("request_uri=" + req.getAttribute(RequestDispatcher.ERROR_REQUEST_URI));
        out.println("query_string=" + req.getAttribute(RequestDispatcher.ERROR_QUERY_STRING));
        out.println("servlet_name=" + req.getAttribute(RequestDispatcher.ERROR_SERVLET_NAME));
        out.println("original method=" + req.getAttribute(RequestDispatcher.ERROR_METHOD));
    }
}
Four ways to fail
@WebServlet("/boom")
public class BoomServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void service(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws ServletException, IOException {
        switch (String.valueOf(req.getParameter("kind"))) {
            case "status" -> resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_FORBIDDEN, "no entry");
            case "runtime" -> throw new IllegalStateException("catalogue exploded");
            case "wrapped" -> throw new ServletException("lookup failed", new SQLException("db down"));
            case "committed" -> {
                resp.getWriter().println("partial page");
                resp.flushBuffer();
                throw new IllegalStateException("too late for an error page");
            }
            default -> resp.getWriter().println("kinds: status, runtime, wrapped, committed");
        }
    }
}
B=http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet
for k in status runtime wrapped committed; do curl -si -X POST "$B/boom?kind=$k"; done
curl -si $B/nothing/here
HTTP/1.1 403
error page /errors/generic dispatcher=ERROR handled-as=GET
status=403
message=no entry
exception_type=null
exception=null
request_uri=/g2-servlet/boom
query_string=kind=status
servlet_name=org.example.bookshelf.BoomServlet
original method=POST
HTTP/1.1 500
error page /errors/generic dispatcher=ERROR handled-as=GET
status=500
message=
exception_type=null
exception=java.lang.IllegalStateException: catalogue exploded
request_uri=/g2-servlet/boom
query_string=kind=runtime
servlet_name=org.example.bookshelf.BoomServlet
original method=POST
HTTP/1.1 500
error page /errors/database dispatcher=ERROR handled-as=GET
status=500
message=lookup failed
exception_type=class java.sql.SQLException
exception=java.sql.SQLException: db down
request_uri=/g2-servlet/boom
query_string=kind=wrapped
servlet_name=org.example.bookshelf.BoomServlet
original method=POST
HTTP/1.1 200
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

partial page
curl: (18) transfer closed with outstanding read data remaining
HTTP/1.1 404
error page /errors/generic dispatcher=ERROR handled-as=GET
status=404
message=The requested resource [/g2-servlet/nothing/here] is not available
exception_type=null
exception=null
request_uri=/g2-servlet/nothing/here
query_string=null
servlet_name=default
original method=GET

The outputs teach five things. The POST that failed was handled as GET with the original method in error.method. The servlet_name identifies the component that failed, including default for a missing resource. For an escaped runtime exception that matched the default entry, Tomcat 11 supplied the exception attribute but left exception_type null and the message empty, so an error page should read error.exception. A ServletException wrapping a SQLException reached the /errors/database page through the second, root-cause pass; the status was 500 in both. And when the response was already committed (committed), no error page can run: the client got the partial page and a truncated chunked body (curl exits with 18), which is the visible symptom of an exception after a flush.

When the same web.xml also declared <exception-type>java.lang.Throwable</exception-type>, the result for wrapped changed. That entry matches every exception at the first pass, so the wrapped case never reached /errors/database and produced /errors/generic with exception_type=class java.sql.SQLException: the root-cause pass is skipped whenever a broad type is declared. A catch-all belongs in the entry without code and type.

The error page mechanism does not apply to exceptions thrown inside a RequestDispatcher call or to errors that the calling filter handles itself, so a filter or servlet that dispatches gets the chance to deal with the error first. The error response is also the place to avoid leaking information: Tomcat’s default report shows the exception and the server version unless ErrorReportValve is configured (showReport, showServerInfo), so applications supply their own page and never print stack traces to users.

File Upload: @MultipartConfig and Part

A multipart/form-data request carries several parts, text fields and files. Since Servlet 3.0 the API reads them with getParts() and getPart(name), which return Part objects; no third-party library is needed. A servlet must opt in, with @MultipartConfig or <multipart-config>, or getPart throws.

Table 26. The @MultipartConfig attributes (sizes in bytes since the 6.1 Javadoc clarification, issue 463)
Attribute Meaning

location

Directory for temporary files and for Part.write with a relative name; the default is the container’s temp directory

fileSizeThreshold

Size above which a part is spooled to disk instead of memory

maxFileSize

Maximum size of one part; the default is unlimited, so always set it

maxRequestSize

Maximum size of the whole request; unlimited by default, so always set it
Table 27. The Part API
Method Notes

getName()

The form field name

getSubmittedFileName()

The client’s file name, a hint for display only; browsers send only the file name, but a hostile client can send a path

getContentType()

The client’s claim, not proof of the content

getSize(), getInputStream()

Size and the content stream

getHeader(name), getHeaders(name)

The part headers

write(fileName), delete()

Persist to the location or discard the temporary file

UploadServlet accepts a book cover. It checks the request type, applies the limits through the annotation, treats text fields as ordinary parameters, checks the declared type against an allowlist, ignores the client’s name for storage, and copies the stream to a file name chosen by the server:

A cover upload with limits and a server-chosen file name
@WebServlet("/upload")
@MultipartConfig(location = "", fileSizeThreshold = 8 * 1024, maxFileSize = 64 * 1024, maxRequestSize = 128 * 1024)
public class UploadServlet extends HttpServlet {

    private static final Set<String> TYPES = Set.of("image/png", "image/jpeg");

    @Override
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws ServletException, IOException {
        resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
        String contentType = req.getContentType();
        if (contentType == null || !contentType.toLowerCase().startsWith("multipart/form-data")) {
            resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE, "multipart/form-data expected");
            return;
        }
        Part cover;
        String title;
        try {
            title = req.getParameter("title");               // text fields arrive as ordinary parameters
            cover = req.getPart("cover");
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {                  // size limits exceeded
            resp.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_REQUEST_ENTITY_TOO_LARGE);
            resp.getWriter().println("upload rejected: too large");
            return;
        }
        if (cover == null || cover.getSize() == 0 || !TYPES.contains(cover.getContentType())) {
            resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE, "send a PNG or JPEG in the cover part");
            return;
        }
        String submitted = cover.getSubmittedFileName();     // the client's name: display only, never a file path
        String display = submitted == null ? "" : Paths.get(submitted.replace('\\', '/')).getFileName().toString();
        File dir = (File) getServletContext().getAttribute("jakarta.servlet.context.tempdir");
        Path target = dir.toPath().resolve(UUID.randomUUID() + ".png");     // the server picks the stored name
        try (InputStream in = cover.getInputStream()) {
            Files.copy(in, target);
        }
        resp.getWriter().println("title=" + title + " cover=" + display + " type=" + cover.getContentType()
                + " bytes=" + cover.getSize() + " stored=" + Files.exists(target));
        Files.delete(target);
    }
}
B=http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet
curl -si -F title=Dune -F 'cover=@cover.png;type=image/png;filename=../../etc/dune cover.png' $B/upload
curl -si -F title=Dune -F 'cover=@note.txt;type=text/plain' $B/upload | head -1
curl -si -F title=Dune -F 'cover=@big.png;type=image/png' $B/upload | sed -n '1p;/^$/,$p'
curl -si -d title=x $B/upload | head -1
HTTP/1.1 200
...
title=Dune cover=dune cover.png type=image/png bytes=69 stored=true
HTTP/1.1 415
HTTP/1.1 413

upload rejected: too large
HTTP/1.1 415

The hostile file name ../../etc/dune cover.png was reduced to dune cover.png for display and never used as a path. The text file was refused with 415, the 100 KB image exceeded maxFileSize (64 KB) and the container threw IllegalStateException, which the servlet turned into 413. The last request is not multipart at all. Before the content-type check was added to the servlet, Tomcat answered it with a 500 whose exception was a ServletException wrapping InvalidContentTypeException; the check turns a client mistake into the 415 a client deserves. Uploaded content is still untrusted: verify the magic bytes or decode the image, store it outside the web root, serve it with a fixed content type and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and never execute or include it.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 3.2 File Upload

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 8.1.5 @MultipartConfig

Source: Jakarta EE Tutorial — Uploading Files with Jakarta Servlet Technology

Source: OWASP — File Upload Cheat Sheet

Asynchronous Processing in Brief

A servlet that waits for a slow resource (a remote service, a queue) can release the container thread instead of blocking it. It calls startAsync(), returns, and later completes the response from another thread with AsyncContext.complete() or re-dispatches with AsyncContext.dispatch. Both the servlet and every filter in its path must declare asyncSupported (annotation attribute or <async-supported>), or startAsync throws IllegalStateException. The example’s three timing filters declare it in web.xml.

Releasing the container thread while a slow task runs
@WebServlet(urlPatterns = "/async", asyncSupported = true)
public class AsyncServlet extends HttpServlet {
    @Override
    protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        String requestThread = Thread.currentThread().getName();
        AsyncContext async = req.startAsync();               // the container thread is released when doGet returns
        async.setTimeout(5_000);
        async.start(() -> {
            try {
                Thread.sleep(200);                            // stands in for a slow remote call
                resp.setContentType("text/plain;charset=UTF-8");
                resp.getWriter().println("request thread=" + requestThread + ", worker thread="
                        + Thread.currentThread().getName());
            } catch (IOException | InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            } finally {
                async.complete();                             // always complete, or the request hangs until timeout
            }
        });
    }
}
curl -s http://localhost:18080/g2-servlet/async
request thread=http-nio-18080-exec-37, worker thread=http-nio-18080-exec-30

The request thread and the worker thread are different threads of the container’s pool. The finally block that calls complete() is not optional: a response that is neither completed nor dispatched stays open until the timeout. Non-blocking I/O (ReadListener, WriteListener), HTTP trailers and protocol upgrade (WebSocket) build on the same machinery and are outside this page; HTTP/2 server push, available through newPushBuilder(), is deprecated in 6.1 and optional for containers. For new applications with high concurrency on Java 21, virtual threads and plain blocking servlets are an alternative worth measuring before reaching for the async API.

Source: Jakarta Servlet 6.1 — 2.3.3.3 Asynchronous Processing

Source: Jakarta EE Tutorial — Asynchronous Processing

The Bookshelf End to End: Adding a Book

The pieces above combine in the most common servlet task: a form that creates a record. The whole flow, as one client sees it, touches almost every section of this page: a filter chain, a controller servlet, a session with a CSRF token, a forward to a JSP, a filter wrapper, validation, a 303 redirect and the error pages.

Table 28. The request journey of "add a book"
Step Request What happens

1

GET /books

outer and inner run (REQUEST); BookServlet.doGet creates the session and a CSRF token in it (the SessionTracker logs sessionCreated and session attribute added: csrf), puts the catalogue in the request, and forwards to /WEB-INF/views/books.jsp; FooterFilter (FORWARD) appends the footer

2

POST /books with the token

BookServlet.doPost compares the token in constant time, validates, adds the book to the shared Catalogue and answers 303 with Location: /g2-servlet/books/4

3

GET /books/4

Path info /4 selects the book; the JSP renders it

4

POST /books without the token

sendError(403); the error page mechanism renders /errors/generic as an ERROR dispatch

5

sendError(400)

6

GET /books with Accept: application/json

Same servlet, same data, JSON with Vary: Accept

The trace of step 1 (with the X-Trace header) is the filter chain the figure showed:

outer before REQUEST /g2-servlet/books

sessionCreated, active=4

The view that step 1 forwards to is books.jsp, listed below: it prints each title with c:out (HTML escaping), builds URLs from ${pageContext.request.contextPath}, and carries the token in a hidden field. The BookServlet code was listed in the request section, and the save path (doPost) is:

BookServlet.doPost: token check, validation, Post/Redirect/Get
    protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse resp) throws IOException {
        HttpSession session = req.getSession(false);
        String expected = session == null ? null : (String) session.getAttribute("csrf");
        String actual = req.getParameter("csrf");
        if (expected == null || actual == null
                || !MessageDigest.isEqual(expected.getBytes(), actual.getBytes())) {
            resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_FORBIDDEN, "Missing or invalid CSRF token");
            return;
        }
        String title = req.getParameter("title");
        String author = req.getParameter("author");
        int year;
        try {
            year = Integer.parseInt(req.getParameter("year"));
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            year = -1;
        }
        if (title == null || title.isBlank() || author == null || author.isBlank() || year < 1450) {
            resp.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST, "title, author and a year >= 1450 are required");
            return;
        }
        Book created = Catalogue.of(getServletContext()).add(title.strip(), author.strip(), year);
        // Post/Redirect/Get: 303 tells the client to follow with a GET, so a refresh never re-posts the form.
        resp.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/books/" + created.id(), HttpServletResponse.SC_SEE_OTHER);
    }
books.jsp: the view the controller forwards to
<%@ page contentType="text/html; charset=UTF-8" pageEncoding="UTF-8" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h1>${initParam['catalogue.title']}</h1>
<ul>
<c:forEach var="b" items="${books}">
  <li><a href="${pageContext.request.contextPath}/books/${b.id}"><c:out value="${b.title}"/></a>
      by <c:out value="${b.author}"/> (${b.year})</li>
</c:forEach>
</ul>
<form method="post" action="${pageContext.request.contextPath}/books">
  <input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="<c:out value='${csrf}'/>">
  <input name="title"> <input name="author"> <input name="year" size="4">
  <button>Add</button>
</form>
</body>
</html>
